analysis.one_liner: Requires a binding ethics code, gift rules, and recusal standards for Supreme Court justices.
analysis.headline: Backed by 94 House Democrats and no Republicans, the bill has sat untouched in the House Judiciary Committee since its referral in May 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Supreme Court to adopt an enforceable code of conduct, set limits on gifts and require disclosure of gifts and reimbursements, and expand the rules on when a justice must step aside from a case — including when a party spent money to support the justice's confirmation or gave the justice income or gifts within the past six years. It would create a public complaint process and panels of other judges to review disqualification decisions, and require people and groups filing friend-of-the-court briefs to disclose who funded them.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary litigants and the general public, who currently have no way to formally complain about a justice's conduct and must take on faith that gifts and financial ties do not influence rulings. Anyone facing a well-funded party in a case before a justice with financial or political ties to that party gains a clearer path to ask for the justice's removal from the case.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Supreme Court to issue a code of conduct for its justices within 180 days, with public notice and comment, and to post the code and related rules on its website in a searchable format.

Establishes a formal process for filing sworn complaints about justices, reviewed by a randomly selected panel of five chief circuit judges, which must publish its findings if it does not recommend dismissal.

Requires justices to step aside from cases where a party or its affiliates lobbied on the justice's nomination or confirmation, or gave the justice, their spouse, or minor child income, gifts, or reimbursements within the prior six years.

Requires litigants and amici to disclose to the Court any gifts, income, or reimbursements their side gave to any justice in the previous two years, plus spending on the justice's confirmation — and requires amicus filers to identify their major funders, with an annual audit.
Lets a party file a disqualification motion that the justice must either grant or send to a reviewing panel, rather than deciding alone; for Supreme Court justices, the other justices decide.

analysis.who_pays: The nine Supreme Court justices give up sole discretion over their own recusal and face a formal complaint process, gift limits, and disclosure duties. Wealthy donors and litigants who give justices gifts or fund confirmation efforts would be exposed by disclosure rules. Law firms, advocacy groups, and interest groups that file amicus briefs would have to disclose their major funders.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is largely internal: the Court writes its own code and handles its own complaints, and the investigation panel only presents findings and recommendations to the Supreme Court, which decides what action to take.

The gift rules direct the Counselor to the Chief Justice to set standards matching what members of Congress must follow under current House and Senate rules, rather than imposing an independent, stricter standard.
Some legal scholars argue Congress regulating the internal conduct of the Supreme Court raises separation-of-powers concerns about legislative control over a coequal branch.

The new disclosure requirements for amicus briefs and disqualification notices add paperwork for courts, law firms, and advocacy groups, and require litigants to research and report gift histories of lawyers and parties.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give the public a working process for policing Supreme Court ethics where none exists now, though its design leaves the Court substantial control over its own rules and enforcement, which could blunt its impact. The compliance costs fall on a small number of institutions — the Court, elite law firms, and major amicus filers — while the benefit is broader confidence in the impartiality of the nation's highest court.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has not scheduled a hearing or a vote on it.

narrative.text: Hank Johnson of Georgia introduced the bill on May 20, 2025 with 28 original cosponsors, all House Democrats, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The bill gained 94 Democratic cosponsors in total, but no Republicans.
No further action appears in the record after the referral: no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote have been scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo is preserved: Supreme Court justices continue to write and apply their own ethics rules, and litigants cannot compel a justice's recusal. The organizations and individuals whose gifts and funding would have been disclosed are spared that exposure.

for.name: Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Supreme Court Ethics, Recusal, and Transparency Act of 2025 on May 20, 2025.

for.name: 94 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 28 original cosponsors who joined at introduction.

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since it was referred to the committee in May 2025.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: No House Republican cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 94 cosponsors are House Democrats; not a single House Republican signed on, so the bill's only path would require the Republican-run Judiciary Committee to act, which it has not.

industries.note: The bill strips justices of sole authority over their own recusal and gifts, and exposes them to formal complaints and mandatory disclosure. Justices' current discretion over their own ethics is exactly what the bill removes.

industries.industry: Law firms and advocacy groups that file amicus briefs
industries.note: The bill requires amicus filers to identify anyone who funded at least 3% of their revenue, over $100,000, or helped prepare the brief, with an annual audit. The cost is compliance paperwork, but the disclosure removes the ability to influence the Court without the public seeing who is behind the argument.

Litigants and their lawyers would have to disclose any gifts, income, or reimbursements given to a justice within two years, and any spending to support the justice's confirmation. Donors who benefit from a justice's continued role in a case would be identified.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing scheduled and no Republican support, which historically means it will not advance in this Congress; its realistic path is re-introduction in a future Congress under a different majority.
